one_liner: Fails the quality test (weak financial health), so price does not matter.

profile.what: Microchip Technology supplies microcontrollers, analog and mixed-signal chips, and programmable logic devices to a very broad range of industrial, automotive, aerospace and data-centre customers.
profile.money: It sells large numbers of inexpensive chips, each designed into a customer's product for years. No single customer or product accounts for much of its revenue.
profile.valued: Microchip is valued on forward P/E and EV/EBITDA as a cyclical chipmaker. Investors watch order trends, customer inventories and the pace of debt reduction.

summary.sentence: A sticky microcontroller franchise recovering from a severe inventory bust, with debt and a stretched dividend.
strengths: Debt has been reduced every year in the record.
risks: Revenue fell by more than two fifths in fiscal 2025.
Dividends have exceeded free cash flow in the last two fiscal years.
Earnings cover interest fewer than four times.

meaning.what_it_does: Makes microcontrollers and analog chips that go into industrial equipment, cars, appliances and data-centre hardware.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Sells many thousands of low-cost chips to a very wide base of customers, mostly through distributors.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Once a chip is designed into a product it is rarely replaced, and Microchip seldom discontinues a part.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Another deep inventory correction, with heavy debt and a dividend it struggles to cover.

moat.summary: Customers rarely redesign around a working microcontroller, but several large rivals offer comparable parts.

industry.summary: Microcontrollers change slowly, but orders swing sharply with customers' inventories.

management.summary: Built through debt-funded acquisitions; kept paying the dividend through a severe downturn while cutting costs.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $724M a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 3–9% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 16%; cost of capital 9.0%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
